title: RSGI's second Harvey report shows jump in adoption
author: Legal IT Insider

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s core view of Harvey as emerging legal-work infrastructure rather than merely a productivity tool. It also reinforces the practical emphasis on adoption, integration and capability-building, while treating employment expansion as a tentative interpretation rather than a demonstrated outcome.
qs: Harvey is becoming the infrastructure on which legal work is built.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account that AI is becoming embedded in legal workflows and that benefits depend on organisational adoption, integration and capability-building rather than tool access alone. It also aligns with the cluster’s cautious labour-market conclusion by presenting demand expansion, rather than lawyer displacement, as a possibility rather than a demonstrated result. It does not materially address verification or apprenticeship risks.
qs: The Jevons Paradox may be at work: increased efficiency is enabling more work to be done, not fewer lawyers to be employed.*  To compare and contrast last year’s report, see [here](https://www.harvey.ai/resources/reports/harvey-rsgi-report)  RSGI’s founder and executive director Reena SenGupta said: “The speed and depth of change we are documenting, in just six months, is extraordinary.

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: The source supports the proposition that value depends on effective adoption rather than access or usage volume alone. It reports stronger impact among customers investing in integration and capability-building, and emphasises outcomes and higher-value work as measures of value. Its commissioned, customer-only sample and the limited pass-through of savings constrain broader or causal conclusions but do not undermine the core position.
qs: Most law firms (77%) cite better outcomes as how they justify their Harvey licence spend, and 68% of in-house legal teams point to the ability to focus on higher-value work as their key measure of value.*  *• The proportion of organisations with 30% or more power users has risen from a third (34%) to half (50%) in six months.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s qualified account: it reports substantial agent deployment, workflow integration and perceived capacity gains, while disclosing that the research covered Harvey customers and was commissioned by Harvey. It therefore evidences commercial and operational traction but does not establish independent legal performance or durable defensibility.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s core view that AI is producing task and organisational gains while reshaping, rather than wholesale replacing, legal work. Its reported time, utilisation and profitability improvements are limited to surveyed Harvey users and partly to firms able to track outcomes, while scarce client cost savings and largely stable near-term hiring plans reinforce the distinction between adoption, realised value and labour substitution. It also supports workflow integration and capability-building as prerequisites, though it offers little evidence on verification or the jagged capability frontier.

kp.k: Harvey-commissioned research tracks customer adoption over six months
kp.d: Legal IT Insider reports on RSGI’s second Harvey study, released on June 17, 2026, building on its November 2025 report. Both studies were commissioned by Harvey and described as independently conducted by RSGI. Research between April and June 2026 covered 87 unique respondents across 60 firms and 27 in-house teams; its two streams were a quantitative survey of 82 respondents and 54 long-form qualitative interviews. The participating organisations spanned multiple regions, firm sizes and corporate sectors.
qs: Both were commissioned by Harvey, but carried out on an independent basis by RSGI.
draws on research conducted between April and June 2026, comprising 87 unique respondents across 60 firms and 27 in-house teams.

The research was conducted between April and June 2026 and comprised two streams: a quantitative survey of 82 respondents (57 law firms and 25 in-house legal teams) and 54 long-form qualitative interviews of 45–75 minutes each.
Law firms ranged from boutiques to global elite firms across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, the UK and Latin America.

kp.k: Agent deployment and integrations expand Harvey’s operational role
kp.d: The reported findings indicate that 68% of law firms and in-house teams already deploy Harvey-based AI agents, while 21% of law firms run more than 50 agents in production. Integrations with document management systems, Microsoft 365 and MCP/API are described as important changes in use.
qs: 68% of law firms and in-house teams are already deploying Harvey-based AI agents, with over a fifth (21%) of law firms running more than 50 agents in production.
Integration with document management systems, Microsoft 365 and MCP/API are described as “gamechangers.”

kp.k: Firms report increased capacity, time savings and financial gains
kp.d: Among surveyed law firms, 89% say Harvey enables them to take on more work. Reported average weekly time savings for law-firm power users rose from 8.5 to 11 hours over six months. Among firms able to track changes, 59% report increased lawyer utilisation, 44% increased revenue and 53% increased profitability in lawyers using Harvey; these financial findings are expressly limited to firms able to track changes.
qs: 89% of law firms say they can take on more work because of Harvey.
Power users at law firms now save an average of 11 hours per week, up from 8.5 hours six months ago.
Among firms able to track changes, 59% report increased lawyer utilisation, 44% increased revenue, and 53% increased profitability in lawyers that use Harvey.

kp.k: Value measures shift toward outcomes and higher-value work
kp.d: The report characterises a shift over six months toward measuring value through legal and commercial outcomes. Better outcomes justify Harvey licence spending for 77% of law firms, while 68% of in-house teams identify the ability to focus on higher-value work as their key value measure.
qs: Value is now measured in better legal and commercial outcomes, a significant leap from six months ago.

Most law firms (77%) cite better outcomes as how they justify their Harvey licence spend, and 68% of in-house legal teams point to the ability to focus on higher-value work as their key measure of value.

kp.k: Power-user penetration grows, with reported rapid skill development
kp.d: The share of organisations with at least 30% power users increased from 34% to 50% in six months. Asked about becoming a power user, 57% of law firms and 70% of in-house teams say a lawyer can do so in under three months.
qs: The proportion of organisations with 30% or more power users has risen from a third (34%) to half (50%) in six months.
Fluency is achievable quickly: 57% of law firms and 70% of in-house teams say a lawyer can become a power user in under three months.

kp.k: Harvey increasingly described as foundational legal delivery infrastructure
kp.d: The report states that 55% of law firms and 48% of in-house teams now describe Harvey as a foundational technology rather than a tool. RSGI’s Reena SenGupta interprets this as emerging AI enablement. Harvey’s K-Ming Lee separately argues that the greatest impact occurs in organisations investing in adoption, integration and capability-building, and frames AI enablement as a competitive advantage.
qs: Over half of all respondents have moved from using Harvey as a tool to describing it as a foundational technology on which their legal services delivery is built – 55% of law firms and 48% of in-house legal teams.
Harvey is becoming the infrastructure on which legal work is built. Firms and legal teams are showing real signs of AI enablement.

The organization seeing the greatest impact are those investing in adoption, integration and capability-building, demonstrating that AI enablement is becoming a core competitive advantage across the legal sector.

kp.k: Client efficiency discussions diverge from reported savings
kp.d: The report contrasts 61% of law firms saying they proactively discussed Harvey efficiencies with clients against only 4% of in-house teams reporting such approaches from their firms. Although 48% of in-house teams mandated law-firm AI use, only one reported receiving resulting cost savings.
qs: 61% of law firms say they have proactively discussed Harvey efficiencies with clients.
Only 4% of in-house teams say their law firms have approached them about this.
Almost half (48%) of in-house teams have mandated their law firms to use AI, yet only one reported receiving cost savings as a result.

kp.k: AI skills reshape hiring criteria and lawyer appraisals
kp.d: Reported changes extend to recruitment and formal evaluation: 82% of law firms and 94% of in-house teams are changing hiring criteria to prioritise AI skills. AI competency has entered formal partner appraisals at 23% of law firms and associate appraisals at 33%.
qs: Almost all law firms (82%) and in-house legal teams (94%) are changing hiring criteria to prioritise AI skills.
23% of law firms have introduced AI competency into formal partner appraisals, rising to 33% for associates.

kp.k: Staffing expectations favour stability rather than broad intake cuts
kp.d: Most in-house teams, 68%, expect headcount to remain flat; 69% of law firms are not planning to reduce graduate intake over the next two years. These are expectations and plans, not observed employment outcomes. The document tentatively invokes the Jevons Paradox to suggest that efficiency may enable more work rather than fewer lawyers.
qs: Most in-house teams (68%) expect headcount to remain flat, and 69% of law firms are not planning to reduce graduate intake over the next two years.
The Jevons Paradox may be at work: increased efficiency is enabling more work to be done, not fewer lawyers to be employed.

pts.k: RSGI reports that Harvey adoption is expanding from individual productivity assistance into agents and foundational infrastructure, alongside increased capacity, reported business benefits and changing skills requirements.
pts.d: Legal IT Insider reports RSGI's findings that 68% of surveyed law firms and in-house teams deploy Harvey-based agents, and 21% of law firms run more than 50 agents in production. Some 89% of law firms report capacity for more work; law-firm power users reportedly save 11 hours weekly, compared with 8.5 hours six months earlier. Among firms able to track changes, 59% report higher lawyer utilisation, 44% higher revenue and 53% higher profitability among Harvey users. Better outcomes justify licence spending for 77% of law firms, while 68% of in-house teams use the ability to focus on higher-value work as their key value measure. Organisations with at least 30% power users increased from 34% to 50%; 55% of law firms and 48% of in-house teams describe Harvey as foundational technology. The report also identifies a client-provider reporting gap: 61% of firms say they proactively discussed efficiencies with clients, but only 4% of in-house teams report being approached. Although 48% of in-house teams mandate external firms' AI use, only one reported receiving resulting cost savings. Hiring criteria increasingly prioritise AI skills, and some firms incorporate AI competency into lawyer appraisals. Most in-house teams expect flat headcount, and most law firms do not plan to cut graduate intake. The article suggests, rather than establishes, that increased efficiency may expand work rather than reduce lawyer employment. RSGI's Reena SenGupta describes Harvey as emerging infrastructure for legal work; Harvey's K-Ming Lee claims that organisations investing in adoption, integration and capability-building see the greatest impact and that AI enablement is becoming a competitive advantage.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of RSGI's survey and qualitative interviews with Harvey customers, compared with its previous report; the research was commissioned by Harvey and described as independently conducted.
pts.d: The article identifies 87 unique respondents across 60 law firms and 27 in-house teams overall. Its methodological breakdown specifies a quantitative survey of 82 respondents—57 law firms and 25 in-house teams—and 54 long-form interviews lasting 45–75 minutes. The adoption, benefits, hiring and staffing figures are reported respondent findings. The utilisation, revenue and profitability figures specifically concern firms able to track changes. Comparisons draw on RSGI's first Harvey report, published in November 2025. The article supplies no separate quantitative demonstration of the proposed Jevons Paradox explanation or of Lee's competitive-advantage claim; these are interpretations accompanying the research.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Findings describe April–June 2026 customer experience and changes characterised as occurring over six months; graduate-intake plans cover the next two years.
pts.d: Published on June 17, 2026, the article presents current adoption and reported benefits from research conducted between April and June 2026. It compares those findings with the November 2025 report, describing the interval as six months. Reported weekly time savings apply to law-firm power users, not all lawyers. Some 57% of law firms and 70% of in-house teams say a lawyer can reach power-user status in under three months. Financial and utilisation findings are conditional on firms being able to track changes. The two-year horizon applies explicitly to graduate-intake plans; no equivalent horizon is specified for in-house headcount expectations. The Jevons Paradox explanation is tentative, while Lee conditions the greatest reported impact on investment in adoption, integration and capability-building.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The reported changes affect Harvey-using law firms, corporate legal departments, lawyers, recruits and external-law-firm clients.
pts.d: The sampled firms range from boutiques to global elite firms across several regions; corporate legal teams include Fortune 500 and FTSE 100 companies across multiple industries. Law firms report increased capacity and business benefits, while in-house teams emphasise higher-value work and generally expect stable headcount. Clients mandate AI use but rarely report receiving associated cost savings in this sample. AI skills increasingly affect recruitment: 82% of law firms and 94% of in-house teams are changing hiring criteria. Formal AI competency assessment extends to partners in 23% of firms and associates in 33%. Graduate entrants are affected by staffing plans, with 69% of firms not planning intake reductions over the next two years. These are findings about participating Harvey customers, rather than reported measurements of the entire legal market or public access to justice.
